_note: Every orbital figure here was retrieved from the NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP service, table pscomppars (Planetary Systems Composite Parameters), on 2026-08-19. Nothing is estimated, rounded from memory, or invented. Where the archive returned no value the field is null and the confidence is lowered accordingly. These are SPATIAL TEMPLATES: the geometry is borrowed, the meaning comes from Siddhesh's graph.

systems.geometryBasis: Extremely compact resonant chain. All seven orbits lie inside 0.062 AU — the whole system would fit well inside Mercury's orbit. Spacing ratio outer/inner = 5.4.
systems.visualCharacter: dense, tightly nested, near-equal spacing, everything close to the star
systems.notes: Complete measured geometry for all 7 planets.

systems.geometryBasis: Directly imaged, enormously wide. Outer planet is 4.1x the inner. Spans 16-68 AU.
systems.visualCharacter: vast, sparse, four widely separated bodies, huge negative space
systems.notes: The strongest available contrast to TRAPPIST-1.

systems.geometryBasis: Extreme dynamic range: an ultra-short-period planet at 0.015 AU and a distant giant at 5.6 AU — a 363x span.
systems.visualCharacter: one body almost touching the star, then a huge leap outward
systems.notes: Archive reports sy_pnum 7 but returned geometry for only 5. Two planets lack values in pscomppars.

illustrative._warning: NOT ASTRONOMY. Orbits beyond the fifth are spaced by a declared rule and must never be presented as measured.
illustrative.orbitSpacingRule: successive 3:2 period ratio, a proportional to P^(2/3), step 1.31037 — the same rule Kepler-16 uses, so two worlds do not invent two different conventions
illustrative._whySpacing: The archive reports sy_pnum 7 for 55 Cnc but returns semi-major axes for only 5; the other two lack values in pscomppars. BUSINESS has 7 concepts. Orbits 0-4 are the five real measurements. Orbits 5-6 are spaced by this rule and are NOT measurements — the same treatment Kepler-16's orbits 1-3 receive.

systems.geometryBasis: Strikingly regular near-geometric progression — each orbit roughly 2x the previous.
systems.visualCharacter: orderly, systematic, evenly graded outward — the most 'architectural' spacing available

systems.geometryBasis: Five planets packed inside 0.38 AU, then one distant outlier at 3.11 AU — an 8x jump.
systems.visualCharacter: compact core plus one far-flung body — a system with an outlier

systems.geometryBasis: Remarkably flat and coplanar; five inner planets crowded between 0.09 and 0.25 AU.
systems.visualCharacter: a flat, layered plane — the most 'stratified' system available

systems.geometryBasis: Resonant chain — the outer five are in a 2:4:6:9:12 Laplace resonance.
systems.visualCharacter: rhythmic, synchronised, mathematically periodic motion
systems.notes: The resonance is the reason this is the natural candidate for MUSIC.

systems.geometryBasis: Unbroken 3:2 resonant chain for the inner five, then a gap to the sixth.
systems.visualCharacter: an ordered inner sequence, then a break — progression with a discontinuity

systems.visualCharacter: steady outward growth — each shell slightly larger than the last

systems.geometryBasis: Three outer planets in a Laplace resonance (1:2:4); one very close inner planet.
systems.visualCharacter: coupled bodies whose motions are locked to each other

measured._massSource: primary 0.6897 from pscomppars; secondary 0.20 from the Doyle et al. 2011 abstract ("20% and 69% as massive as the sun")
measured._binarySource: Doyle et al. 2011 abstract: "The eclipsing stars are 20% and 69% as massive as the sun, and have an eccentric 41-day orbit."
measured._coplanarSource: Doyle et al. 2011 abstract: "The motions of all three bodies are confined to within 0.5 degree of a single plane."

derived._formula: Kepler's third law, a^3 = M_total * (P/365.25)^2 in AU / solar masses / years
derived._swingMeaning: the small star swings 3.45x wider than the massive one — they are bound, but they do not move equally
derived._planetMeaning: the planet orbits at 3.15x the stellar separation, so the centre of this system is a large empty region
derived._stabilitySource: Holman & Wiegert 1999 critical semi-major axis for P-type orbits, evaluated at e=0. Because the binary is eccentric the true limit is LARGER than this; this is a lower bound only.
derived._sizeMeaning: cube root of the measured mass ratio, used only to size the two stars relative to each other
derived._tempMeaning: follows from 0.20 < 0.69 solar masses on the main sequence; the secondary Teff itself was NOT measured

illustrative._warning: NOT ASTRONOMY. Chosen for rendering because the measured value could not be sourced. Must never be presented as measured.
illustrative._why: Doyle et al. 2011 states the binary orbit IS eccentric but gives no number in any abstract or archive table reachable here, so the orbit is drawn visibly non-circular at a declared value rather than drawn as a circle, which would contradict the published description.
illustrative.orbitSpacingRule: successive 3:2 period ratio, a ∝ P^(2/3), step 1.31037
illustrative._whySpacing: Kepler-16 has exactly ONE measured planet. LOVE has four Minor IGs. Orbit 0 is the real measured orbit; orbits 1-3 are spaced by this declared rule and are NOT measurements.

unverified.binaryEccentricityValue: no numeric value in NASA pscomppars, the ps table, or any fetchable abstract

systems.geometryBasis: CIRCUMBINARY. Two stars of 0.69 and 0.20 solar masses on an eccentric 41-day mutual orbit, derived separation 0.2238 AU. The single measured planet orbits the PAIR at 0.7048 AU — 3.15x the stellar separation — leaving a large dynamically empty centre.
systems.visualCharacter: two unequal centres swinging anti-phase about a shared barycentre, a wide hollow middle where nothing can hold an orbit, then a small number of far, slow bodies
systems.notes: Planet geometry and primary star from pscomppars (Doyle et al. 2011). Secondary mass, binary period, eccentric-ness and 0.5-degree coplanarity from the Doyle et al. 2011 abstract. Binary semi-major axis and barycentre split DERIVED via Kepler third law. Binary eccentricity value remains UNVERIFIED.

systems.geometryBasis: Five bodies inside 0.08 AU, a 4.5x span — the tightest packing in this set. The periods stand in near whole-number ratios to each other.
systems.visualCharacter: close, ordered, rhythmic — bodies locked to one another rather than merely near one another
systems.notes: Archive reports sy_pnum 6 but returned a semi-major axis for only 5; Kepler-80 g has no pl_orbsmax value in pscomppars.

illustrative._warning: NOT ASTRONOMY. Orbits beyond the fifth are spaced by a declared rule and must never be presented as measured.
illustrative.orbitSpacingRule: successive 3:2 period ratio, a proportional to P^(2/3), step 1.31037 — the same rule Kepler-16 and 55 Cnc use, so no world invents its own convention
illustrative._whySpacing: Orbits 0-4 are the five real measurements. Anything beyond them is spaced by this rule and is NOT a measurement.

systems.geometryBasis: A 13x span with the width concentrated in one place: gaps of 1.68, 1.29, 3.56 and 1.68, so the third step is more than twice any other.
systems.visualCharacter: an inner cluster and a distant pair, with a conspicuous emptiness between them
systems.notes: All five planets returned both a period and a semi-major axis.

systems.geometryBasis: A 12.8x span whose gaps WIDEN outward - 1.71, 1.65, 1.87, 2.43 - the most steadily opening system in this set.
systems.visualCharacter: open and unhurried, each body further from its neighbour than the last
systems.notes: Lettered b, c, d, f, g: the archive returns no e for this host. All five returned both a period and a semi-major axis.

systems.geometryBasis: Three small planets inside 0.15 AU, then Kepler-167 e alone at 1.883 AU — a cold giant beyond the snow line, 13.4x further out than the planet before it. The final gap is wider than the whole inner system.
systems.visualCharacter: a tight inner cluster and one body far outside it, with nothing at all in between
systems.notes: All four axes agree with Kepler’s third law to within 0.06% under the archive’s stellar mass, so the geometry is internally consistent rather than a mix of sources. Two stars in the system (sy_snum 2); the planets orbit the primary, so this is NOT a circumbinary case like Kepler-16.

systems.geometryBasis: Two close planets, then a jump of 16.3x to Kepler-68 d and a further 3.1x to e at 4.6 AU. The system is cut in half by a gap in its MIDDLE rather than at its edge.
systems.visualCharacter: two bodies near the star and two far from it, divided by an empty band that dominates the system
systems.notes: The outermost planet was announced in 2023 and its axis sits 0.96% off the law under the composite stellar mass; the inner three agree to within 0.01%. Two stars (sy_snum 2); the planets orbit the primary.

systems.geometryBasis: Three modest planets already spread across 0.10 to 0.34 AU, then a 6.3x step out to a giant at 2.16 AU. The same family as Kepler-167 and half as extreme: its inner bodies are apart from each other before the outer gap opens.
systems.visualCharacter: an unhurried inner group and a distant giant, around a nearby sun-like star
systems.notes: A G9 V star 22 pc away — the nearest of the six added here, though five systems already in this file are nearer still. All four axes agree with Kepler’s third law to within 0.5%. Discovery spans 2005 to 2021, so the four figures come from four different papers and cohere anyway.

systems.geometryBasis: Eight planets, as many as the Solar System, and no system in the archive has more. Three crowd inside 0.13 AU, one 2.66x step opens a gap, and five more are graded outward to 0.97 AU — the entire system fits inside Earth’s orbit.
systems.visualCharacter: the fullest system there is: a crowded core, one clear break, and a long ordered outer run
systems.notes: THIS CLOSES A GAP RECORDED IN THIS FILE. The earlier attempt queried hostname ‘Kepler-90’ and got nothing back; the archive files the system under KOI-351, and only the planet found in 2017 carries the Kepler-90 name. Confidence is medium because five of the eight axes are quoted to two significant figures and disagree with Kepler’s law by up to 7.6% under the composite stellar mass — the ratios are measured, but coarser than every other system here.

systems.geometryBasis: Five planets between 0.0418 and 0.0811 AU. The total range is 1.9x and every gap falls between 1.16 and 1.23 — the narrowest and most even system in this file by a wide margin.
systems.visualCharacter: five bodies almost sharing a single ring; a world with no outside
systems.notes: The archive gives the star an age of 11.23 Gyr (+0.91/-0.99), older than any other host here and roughly four fifths the age of the universe. Three stars in the system (sy_snum 3): the planets orbit the primary, with a close pair of small stars further out, so this is not circumbinary either.

systems.geometryBasis: Six planets whose spacing widens as it goes: 2.18, then 1.22, 1.91, 2.00, and finally 4.57 out to 3.71 AU. Reach accelerates rather than growing steadily.
systems.visualCharacter: six bodies leaving the star at an increasing pace, ordered but never regular
systems.notes: The inner five axes sit a uniform 2.74–3.02% above the value Kepler’s law gives under the archive’s composite stellar mass, which means axes and mass were taken from different papers. A uniform offset cancels exactly in a ratio, and ratios are all this project renders — but the figures are not one self-consistent solution, and that is why it is recorded here rather than left to be noticed.

_retrieved_2026_09_08: SIX RESERVE SYSTEMS, held for regions that do not exist yet. Kepler-167, Kepler-68, HD 164922, Kepler-90 (archive hostname KOI-351), Kepler-444 and HD 191939, retrieved from the same TAP service and the same table as every other system here. They carry reserve:true and are deliberately absent from MIG_SYSTEM. WHY SIX AND WHY THESE: a world is chosen for a spacing regime the others do not occupy, so the candidates were ranked by distance from the nearest system already spoken for, in a shape space of mean gap, evenness, whether the gaps open or close, the largest single gap and the total reach. Choosing the top six would have taken five near-copies of one shape, so they were picked farthest-point: each is the most unlike everything already chosen, including the ones chosen just before it. Their total reach comes out 1.9x, 13.1x, 21.0x, 39.0x, 46.1x and 75.0x, and they offer 4, 4, 4, 5, 6 and 8 orbits, because a template’s planet count IS the number of rings a region gets and a pool that only offers four can only dress one size of region.
